project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.

constraints: The lignin is currently fired internally as fuel, so redirecting it to a saleable product may displace an existing fuel use.
The mill has no lignin dryer; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying capability or an external drying step.
The mill has no solvent or membrane fractionation or chemical-modification equipment.
The stream leaves as wet cake, and uncertain moisture affects dry tonnage and shipped mass.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are missing, limiting pathway and buyer-specification screening.
data_quality_notes: The mill and feedstock are fictional; all reported figures are illustrative assumptions, not measurements, and must not be used for real decisions.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium content are unreported.
The lignin-content analytical method needs confirmation; moisture is marked uncertain, and reported ranges are assumed variability.
The validator passed the dry-matter balance, composition-total, and missing-figure/data-gap checks; it reported no inconsistencies.
agent.summary: Fictional demo profile: 40,000.0 t/yr wet cake at a moisture fraction of 0.35000000000000003 corresponds to 26,000.0 t/yr dry mass. Validation found no inconsistencies, but the invented figures and listed data gaps preclude relying on this profile for commercial decisions.

lignin_pct.method: Acid-insoluble (Klason) plus acid-soluble lignin, as % of dry matter (method stated for illustration)

sulfur_pct.method: Total sulfur by elemental analysis (stated for illustration)

carbohydrates_pct.method: Total sugars after acid hydrolysis (stated for illustration)

checks.detail: recorded dry matter 26,000 t/yr; wet quantity x (1 - moisture) = 26,000 t/yr
lignin + ash + carbohydrates = 96.5% of dry matter
3 missing figure(s), each with a data-gap entry

data_gaps.impact: Every figure in this profile is invented for demonstration. Results based on it say nothing about a real mill.
data_gaps.next_step: Replace the profile with the mill's own lab data and production records.

data_gaps.impact: Molecular weight can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of molecular weight distribution, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: Phenolic hydroxyl content can't be compared with any pathway requirement until it is measured.
data_gaps.next_step: Commission a lab analysis of hydroxyl group content, and record the method used.

data_gaps.impact: The make-up of the ash is unknown, so ash-related requirements can only be checked against total ash.
data_gaps.next_step: Request an inorganic element analysis of the ash.

data_gaps.impact: Reported lignin content depends on what the analysis counts. The method here is stated for illustration only.
data_gaps.next_step: Confirm the analytical method with the lab and use the same one when comparing with buyers' specifications.

data_gaps.impact: Moisture sets the dry tonnage (dry matter = wet quantity x (1 - moisture)) and the mass that has to be shipped.
data_gaps.next_step: Log cake moisture for each shift over at least one month.

checks.disclaimer: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.

current_use.description: Fictional: the precipitated lignin is fired in the mill's own boilers in place of purchased fuel. The unit was built to relieve the recovery boiler, not to sell lignin.

geographic_market.logistics: Fictional: rail siding at the mill; the nearest deep-water port is assumed to be about 150 km away.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#3: A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins for plywood and other wood-based-panel adhesives, after activation or depolymerization.
Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is also documented for veneer plywood; UPM reports its resin meets the plywood bonding standard named in the source.

target_customers.statement: Plywood manufacturers, including veneer-plywood producers, are the clearest implied customers; the evidence also points to producers of other wood-based panels.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol used in phenol-formaldehyde resin is the incumbent material being replaced.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin.
UPM reports its LPF resin meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood and reports formaldehyde emissions measured under EN 717-2.

A laboratory study reports that resin containing depolymerized lignin at half of the phenolic component met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study; the paper names that standard inconsistently.

limitations: The reported high replacement levels and industrial performance include manufacturer claims; the UPM document does not identify its lignin as kraft or provide its composition.
The laboratory result used poplar plywood, and the standard is named inconsistently in the paper.
The cited TRL 8 assessment is from a 2018 report and applies to biobased phenolic resins generally, not specifically to kraft lignin.
missing_information: No current regional demand, named buyers, purchase prices, contract terms, or buyer volumes are provided.
The evidence does not establish whether Pinecrest's wet cake meets a prospective buyer's composition, moisture, or other specifications, or quantify the needed processing and drying costs.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence includes an industrially proven LPF product claim and established performance testing, but it does not document commercial sales to buyers; this best fits documented industry development evidence rather than the rubric's sales levels.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-05#1: Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.

applications.statement: Lignin has been studied as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyol in rigid polyurethane/polyisocyanurate foam.
Unmodified lignin has also been tested as a partial polyol replacement in flexible polyurethane foam; the study suggests kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses.
Reviews also describe lignin uses in polyurethane panels, coatings, and rubber replacement, though the supplied evidence gives more product-specific performance results for foams.

target_customers.statement: Rigid-foam formulators and producers are implied by the rigid PUR/PIR foam studies.
Flexible-foam producers serving automotive or heavy-duty applications are implied by the study's application discussion.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material lignin is tested to replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: For rigid polyurethane foam production, one source cites a total hydroxyl value above 200 mg KOH/g as an acceptable range; it cautions this is total OH, not phenolic OH.
In one study, rigid foams made with lignin replacement were assessed against ASTM C1029-15 Type 1 specifications.
Kraft lignin generally needs treatment such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction to reach target polyurethane properties, according to the review.

limitations: Most performance evidence is from laboratory foam studies, and rigid-foam results vary across lignins; kraft-specific performance is not consistently isolated.
The polyurethane TRL cited by the review applies to several lignin uses collectively, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam.

A moderate-quality review was available only as an abstract. The library also contains a low-quality synthetic record claiming large-scale sales, which conflicts with the other commercialization evidence and is not relied on here.
missing_information: No named buyers, current regional demand, commercial purchase prices, contract terms, or buyer volumes are provided.
No evidence establishes whether Pinecrest's lignin meets foam-buyer specifications or quantifies modification, drying, and scale-up costs.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence is primarily research and review literature, with a general technology-readiness assessment but no reliable documented commercial sales or specific buyer pilots for kraft-lignin polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.

applications.statement: Lignin is being developed as a precursor for carbon fiber, including lightweighting applications; reported project results cover precursor-fiber production rather than the full lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain.
Kraft lignin-derived hard carbon is discussed for sodium-ion battery anodes; separate company material describes lignin-based anode material for lithium-ion batteries.
Lignin can also be converted to activated carbon, including lignin too impure for other uses; higher ash is reported to reduce yield and carbon conversion.

target_customers.statement: Carbon-fiber producers serving lightweighting applications are implied by the carbon-fiber development evidence.
Battery manufacturers and carmakers are identified as parties involved in qualifying lignin-based anode materials.
Activated-carbon manufacturers are implied by the evidence on producing activated carbon from lignin.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based fiber is named as a comparator for lignin-based carbon fiber.
Anthracite is named as a competing hard-carbon feedstock for sodium-ion batteries.
Conventional activated carbon is the incumbent material identified for this pathway.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content above 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The examined kraft lignin required purification for carbon-fiber use; softwood lignin may need a plasticizing agent to melt-spin, though that observation is not specific to kraft lignin.
Battery-material qualification with manufacturers and carmakers is reported to take 3 years; no battery-anode material specification is given in that source.
For activated carbon, the source reports no strict precursor-quality limitations, while lower ash improves yield; it gives no formal qualification standard.

limitations: The carbon-fiber precursor specifications are stringent, cited secondhand, and do not apply to hard carbon or activated carbon; one study's lignin was not from standard kraft pulping.
The carbon-fiber project reports precursor spinning readiness, not readiness of the full production chain, and its cost estimate is modelled.
Hard-carbon evidence is review-based and limited to sodium-ion battery applications; the battery pilot information is company material with plans whose later status was not verified.
Activated-carbon evidence is from a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: No current regional demand, named buyers, purchase contracts, or buyer volumes are provided for these pathways.

No evidence establishes Pinecrest's suitability for the distinct carbon-fiber, battery-anode, or activated-carbon specifications; current product prices and project-specific processing costs are not provided.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents a precursor-fiber development project reaching an industrially relevant environment and a company-announced pilot line for anode material, consistent with development and pilot evidence; it does not establish commercial sales to established buyers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in phenol-formaldehyde resin; Pinecrest lacks chemical-modification equipment and a lignin dryer, so processing or outside services would be needed.
The deterministic feedstock-compatibility check returned no score because the evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway.
The economics scenarios could not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, or gross contribution because product yield, product price, and variable costs were not supplied.

technical_maturity.statement: The LignoBoost-plus-resin route is reported at TRL 9; this is pathway-level evidence, not proof that Pinecrest's wet cake is qualified.

adoption_barriers.statement: Prospective panel and plywood customers would need to qualify the resin; the evidence reports bonding and formaldehyde-emission testing, but no Pinecrest-specific buyer qualification.
The mill must weigh a saleable route against lignin's existing internal fuel use, and the profile lacks molecular-weight and phenolic-hydroxyl data relevant to buyer screening.
Regional demand, named buyers, prices, contracts, and volumes are not established in the market findings.

missing_inputs: Pinecrest composition and moisture specification fit
assumptions: The scenario analysis uses fictional wet-feedstock mass assumptions of 36,000 / 40,000 / 43,000 t/yr, moisture assumptions of 40 / 35 / 30%, and availability assumptions of 40 / 50 / 60%, respectively, for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The assessment assumes no unreported drying, activation/depolymerization, or customer-qualification assets are available.
The market route is considered potentially feasible with investment or a partner; no buyer commitment is assumed.
uncertainties: No Pinecrest-specific resin performance, dry-basis composition, or buyer specification match has been established.
The evidence's commercial maturity does not resolve the mill's missing modification and drying capability or the uncertain net value versus internal fuel use.
No TRL is specific to this mill's feedstock or implementation.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: A documented resin route and implied panel customers make commercialization plausible, but activation/depolymerization, drying, buyer qualification, and investment or a partner are needed; local buyers and economics remain unconfirmed.

feedstock_compatibility.rationale: The evidence library has no numeric requirements for this pathway to check against.

technical_readiness.rationale: TRL 9 maps to 5. Stated in EV-PF-03#1.

indicative_economics.rationale: Gross contribution per tonne could not be calculated. Missing inputs: product yield, product price, variable costs.

processing_requirements.statement: For carbon-fiber precursor, the cited requirements include lignin content above 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatile material below 5% at 250 °C, residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm, and removal of particulates larger than 1 µm; the examined kraft lignin also required purification.
For activated carbon, the evidence reports no strict precursor-quality limitations, while lower ash improves yield; no formal qualification standard is provided.

The deterministic carbon-fiber-precursor compatibility score is 1; checked feedstock values were lignin content 94% against a minimum of 99%, and ash 1% against a maximum of 0.1%. These checks apply to carbon-fiber precursor, not necessarily the other carbon products.

Pinecrest has no lignin dryer; this is a processing gap for pathways requiring dry powder, while required processing and qualification differ across carbon fiber, battery anodes, and activated carbon.
The economics scenarios could not calculate product output, revenue, variable cost, or gross contribution because product yield, product price, and variable costs were not supplied.

technical_maturity.statement: Lignin precursor-fiber production is reported to have reached TRL 5 in an industrially relevant environment; the cited result covers precursor-fiber production, not the full lignin-to-carbon-fiber chain or the other carbon-material products.

adoption_barriers.statement: Carbon-fiber use faces substantial feedstock purification and specification requirements; Pinecrest's checked lignin content and ash values do not meet the cited precursor limits.
Battery-anode qualification with manufacturers and carmakers is reported to take 3 years, and the source provides no battery-anode material specification.

Activated carbon is described as less restrictive on precursor quality, but there is no formal qualification standard or Pinecrest-specific product performance, and lower ash is associated with improved yield.
No regional buyers, contracts, purchase prices, or volumes are established, and the mill's current internal fuel use is a competing use for the lignin.

assumptions: The scenario analysis uses fictional wet-feedstock mass assumptions of 36,000 / 40,000 / 43,000 t/yr, moisture assumptions of 40 / 35 / 30%, and availability assumptions of 40 / 50 / 60%, respectively, for conservative / base / optimistic cases.
The compatibility result is specific to carbon-fiber precursor checks; it is not treated as a compatibility score for battery anodes or activated carbon.
The assessment assumes no unreported purification, drying, or carbon-conversion assets or partners are available.
uncertainties: Carbon materials combines distinct products with different processing, specifications, qualification routes, and markets; one pathway-level score cannot establish fit for each product.
The available compatibility check covers only two numeric precursor requirements, while other specification fields are not reported for Pinecrest.
No pathway-specific price, yield, processing cost, buyer demand, or qualification outcome has been established.

commercialization_feasibility.rationale: The pathway spans products with plausible markets, but key processing assets, buyers, and project economics are not identified; carbon-fiber precursor compatibility is poor and battery qualification is lengthy. Activated carbon may present a less restrictive route, but its fit and economics are unproven.

main_drivers: Only pathway ranked: it met the assessed-weight threshold with 0.8 of criterion weight assessed; indicative economics remains unassessed.
TRL 5 supports a technical-readiness score of 3, and pilot/development evidence supports market-evidence score 3.
Feedstock compatibility scored 1 based on a large gap across two checked carbon-fiber precursor requirements; the check does not establish fit for activated carbon or anode products.

Commercialization feasibility scored 2 because processing assets, buyers, and project economics are not established. Evidence quality was strongest high, with three high- and two moderate-quality records.
what_could_change_it: Measure Pinecrest lignin against specifications for each distinct carbon product, especially activated-carbon and anode requirements; better fit could improve compatibility, while poor fit would reinforce the low score.
Obtain product-specific yields, prices, and variable costs to assess indicative economics and determine whether net value can compete with the existing fuel use.
Secure buyer qualification criteria, a named partner, and a process/equipment plan; these could improve commercialization feasibility or reveal additional barriers.

main_drivers: Insufficient data for ranking: only 0.55 of criterion weight is assessed, below the engine's 0.6 minimum; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics are unassessed, not poor.

what_could_change_it: Measure Pinecrest composition, moisture, and resin-relevant properties against prospective buyer specifications; this would enable feedstock-compatibility assessment.
Establish product yield, price, and variable costs, including drying and activation/depolymerization, to assess economics.
Obtain buyer trials or qualification results and specific purchase terms; evidence of acceptance or unmet requirements could change market and commercialization assessments.

main_drivers: Insufficient data for ranking: only 0.55 of criterion weight is assessed, below the engine's 0.6 minimum; feedstock compatibility and indicative economics are unassessed, not poor.
TRL 9 scored 5, but market evidence scored 2 and commercialization feasibility scored 2; commercial examples do not establish qualification of Pinecrest lignin.

validation_steps.action: Characterize representative wet-cake samples for moisture, molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, sodium, and other product-relevant properties; obtain buyer specification sheets for resin, polyurethane, and each carbon product.
validation_steps.reason: Resolve the missing feedstock properties and enable compatibility assessments, particularly for resins and polyurethanes where compatibility is currently unassessed.

validation_steps.action: Run bench or pilot conversion trials for candidate products and measure dry-basis yield, product quality, and process requirements, including drying and any modification or activation.
validation_steps.reason: Establish Pinecrest-specific technical fit and yield rather than relying on pathway-level maturity evidence.

validation_steps.action: Request written quotes, trial interest, qualification requirements, and potential volumes from prospective buyers and technical partners in each pathway.
validation_steps.reason: Replace general market-development evidence with buyer-specific demand, price, terms, and acceptance information.

validation_steps.action: Build pathway-specific contribution estimates using measured yields, buyer prices, variable processing costs, transport/drying costs, and the value of displaced internal fuel.
validation_steps.reason: Indicative economics is unassessed for all pathways, and net value must account for the existing fuel use and wet-cake handling.
addresses: opportunity cost of internal fuel use

ranking_changers: Pinecrest-specific compatibility and qualification data, especially for phenolic resins and polyurethanes, could make either pathway rankable and alter the shortlist substantially.
Measured product yields, credible buyer prices, and variable processing costs could change pathway economics and overall attractiveness; these inputs are currently missing across all pathways.
Evidence of a committed buyer or partner and a viable drying/modification/equipment route could materially change commercialization feasibility.
Product-specific suitability evidence could distinguish among carbon fiber precursor, battery anode, and activated carbon, which are grouped together in the current carbon-materials pathway.
caveats: The Pinecrest feedstock assessment is explicitly fictional; findings should be treated as a dashboard assessment, not a verified mill-specific conclusion.

The engine ranked carbon materials first, while phenolic resins and polyurethanes are listed as insufficient data, not as lower-ranked options. Their assessed-weight share is below the minimum threshold.
Attractiveness values and ranges are engine outputs, not direct commercial returns. Indicative economics was not assessed for any pathway because product yield, price, and variable costs are missing.

Carbon-materials compatibility is based on only two checked precursor requirements and should not be generalized to activated carbon or battery-anode products; pathway-level TRL evidence also does not prove Pinecrest feedstock qualification.
report.summary: Carbon materials is the sole ranked pathway, at rank 1, but its low feedstock-compatibility and commercialization-feasibility scores and unassessed economics make that ranking provisional. Phenolic resins and polyurethanes remain unranked for insufficient assessed data, not because their unassessed criteria are unfavorable. Prioritize Pinecrest-specific characterization, buyer qualification, and yield/cost evidence before committing to a route.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
A 2018 report cited by the IEA estimates the technology readiness level (TRL) for producing biobased phenolic resins at 8.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
Commercialization of lignin-based polyurethane foams remains limited by low product consistency, poor technical performance, and high production costs.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
Lignin-based polyurethane foams are already sold commercially at large scale (TRL 9).
